extracted.intended_audience: IP litigators, patent attorneys, in-house counsel, and others involved in software patent prosecution and litigation (primarily US-focused)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and lessons for litigating and prosecuting software patents in the United States after the Supreme Court's Alice decision, focusing on §101 patent-eligibility challenges and related strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice two-part test for software patents (35 U.S.C. §101)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the two-part test a court must first consider whether the patent claims are directed to a patent ineligible concept such as an abstract idea, and if so, the court should consider whether the claim’s other elements transform the claim into a patent eligible concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Known ideas are abstract; reciting the use of a conventional computer in the claims to implement the known idea does not make the claim patentable subject matter. The two-step framework is the baseline legal standard for evaluating software patent eligibility under Alice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider Alice in every software-patent litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Alice should be considered in every software patent litigation: since Alice, software patents are routinely challenged under §101, often early in litigation via dispositive motions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because Alice-based challenges became ubiquitous and often successful, every patentee asserting a software patent must evaluate the risk of an Alice challenge and every defendant accused of infringing should consider filing an Alice motion early (often as an early dispositive motion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice analysis relies on claim characterization and may not require evidentiary proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal analysis of software patents under Alice differs from other legal analysis: while the Federal Rules of Evidence govern litigation, under Alice a court must first determine if the claim encompasses an abstract idea, and that first determination is a question of law that often does not require evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts frequently rely on a characterization of the claims rather than the precise claim language; attorney argument is often sufficient, and courts commonly make Alice findings without supporting evidence. Terminology, claim length, or complexity often do not change the analysis. Anti-pattern: assuming that a voluminous evidentiary record or detailed claim wording will prevent an Alice dismissal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Alice to seek quick resolution by avoiding complex invalidity inquiries
rubrics_metrics.description: Alice allows defendants to seek invalidity of software patents by arguing abstractness instead of conducting fact-intensive novelty/obviousness/enablement inquiries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because proving obviousness/enablement/anticipation can require extensive discovery and technical evidence, Alice provides a faster path—show the claim is an abstract idea or combines only conventional elements (including a conventional computer). Combining conventional elements does not make a claim patentable. Strategic guidance: identify conventional methodologies and conventional computer implementation, and argue preemption/breadth to pursue early dispositive relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim breadth and preemption are indicators of abstractness
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim is broad enough to encompass (or preempt) all embodiments of an idea, that is an indicator that the claim is abstract (and thus unpatentable under Alice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broad claims that purport to monopolize an abstract idea also raise enablement concerns (doubtful that the specification enables every possible variation). Under Alice a defendant can emphasize overbreadth/preemption as evidence the claim is an abstract attempt to monopolize an idea rather than a patent-eligible invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice outcomes are unpredictable and inconsistently applied
rubrics_metrics.description: While courts consistently apply the two-part test, the results are unpredictable — similar patents may be found patentable in one court and unpatentable in another, and the application of Alice has been described as 'excessively incoherent, inconsistent and chaotic.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The USPTO and the Federal Circuit have issued guidance and decisions attempting to bring consistency (e.g., guidance to keep 101 rejections distinct from 102/103/112), but courts are not bound by USPTO guidance and the Federal Circuit's efforts have limited effect. Practitioners should plan for uncertainty and differing local-court or panel outcomes; ultimate clarity may require action by the Supreme Court or Congress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second-step factual inquiry can affect the viability of early Alice motions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Circuit has held that the second part of the Alice analysis may require a factual inquiry in some circumstances, which can limit the effectiveness of early dispositive Alice motions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a factual inquiry is required, courts may deny or defer early motions and permit discovery, making it harder for defendants to obtain early dismissal. Some courts still determine no factual inquiry is necessary for the particular case; assess whether the claimed invention's additional elements raise disputed factual issues before filing an early §101 motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-Alice trend: declining success of Alice challenges due to better claims and USPTO scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: Since 2015 the percentage of successful Alice challenges has dropped each year; recent software patents are more likely to survive Alice because patentees draft better claims and the USPTO scrutinizes claims for patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentees should improve claim drafting and consider Alice issues during prosecution; courts may defer to the USPTO's determination on Alice if the issue was considered during prosecution. For defendants, recognize that Alice motions may be less likely to succeed against recently issued, well-drafted software patents and weigh the economics of pursuing §101 challenges.
